content:
Hi all!

I am a PhD in probability theory, currently a postdoc at the university of Zürich. My interests include discrete probability, limit theorems, combinatorics (including generating functionology), graph theory, and quite a lot of Fourier transform.

I learned Lean 3 from the computer scientist's book a few years ago, and did not realize it was a terrible fit before opening Mathlib and - of course - getting immediately lost. Now I am doing it the right way: learning from the Mathematics in Lean book and doing all the exercises. I have covered everything up to chapter 5, and am currently working through Chapter 6 on Finsets and Fintypes.

My interest in Lean is mostly curiosity. I am impressed by the latest news in automated theorem proving and I want to learn more about the topic, and possibly teach about the topic once I have garnered enough expertise. I hope to be able to formalize some of my research results in Lean, and I expect to have to first formalize a bunch of rather-elementary-but-not-quite theories beforehand. So far I have set my sights on

  • proving that random walks converge to the Brownian motion [probability, stochastic processes]
  • establishing a bunch of classical results in concentration of measures [probability]
  • proving a technical lemma on cumulants (sort of moments for random variables) that I love and that I use often in my research [generating functionology, combinatorics, probability]
  • playing with combinatorial (planar) maps, e.g. the Cori-Vauquelin-Schaeffer bijection between quadrangulations and certain decorated trees [graph theory, combinatorics, probability]

Few of them fall within the scope of MathLib, but perhaps some will!

My roadmap before doing so is

  • finish the book
  • explore the library and non-mathlib projects related to the above topics
  • review a few PR to get a feel of how things are done
  • start experimenting :)

I do not use LLMs for coding in Lean. My only use of them will be asking questions when I am stuck, if other, more ethical and frugal alternatives (looking through the library / Zulip / the web) have not born fruit.

Looking forward to talking to you all!
Welcome! It might be interesting for you to look at the #Brownian motion project (Github) and incidentally Rémy will be giving an online talk about related to this tomorrow (see here).
For Fourier theory, you might want to check out YaelDillies/apap (finite abelian groups) and YaelDillies/mean-fourier (compact groups, in progress)
@Jonas Bayer Thank you! I had spotted this project, I intended to look into it once I understood more of how probability theory is implemented in Mathlib. The talk should be a perfect opportunity!
Come on! I want to see combinatorial maps in Mathlib!

@Philippe Duchon Ha! Indeed! That was my motivation for joining the first time :)

I should add it to the list!
That would be awesome. I've tried to get other enumerative combinatorialists interested in Lean, but so far they've all run away before reaching halfway through Mathematics in Lean
